title: Scientific Measurement
standard_text: Scientific measurement: SI units and prefixes; accuracy and precision; significant figures; scientific notation; errors in measurement; unit conversion. (summary of the senior secondary Physics curriculum, SSS 1; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 1 Physics worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): SI units and prefixes, significant figures, scientific notation, accuracy, precision and errors. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated values.
key_sub: Round answers to the right number of significant figures.
body_html:
How to think about it

Scientists measure in SI units (metre, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole) with prefixes such as milli-, centi- and kilo-. Very large or small numbers are written in scientific notation, such as 6.02 × 10²³.

Significant figures show how precise a measurement is. Accurate results are close to the true value; precise results are close to each other. Random errors are reduced by repeating measurements; systematic errors come from the instrument or method.

Example

How many significant figures in 0.00450?

Leading zeros do not count

Answer: 3

Example

Convert 2.5 km to metres.

× 1,000

Answer: 2,500 m

Common mistakes

  • Counting leading zeros as significant.
  • Mixing up accuracy and precision.
  • Forgetting units in answers.

items.e: Mean = 2.50 s. Mean absolute error = average of |ai − amean| = 0.0568 s.

items.q: The radius of a sphere is measured with an error of 3.50%. What is the percentage error in its volume (V = 4πr³/3)?
items.e: For V ∝ r³ the relative error is multiplied by 3: 3 × 3.50% = 10.5%.
